restoreCorrections.definition: Producing, or capable of producing, the intended result.
restoreCorrections.example: The new filter is effective at removing dust.
distinctions: Effective concerns achieving the intended result. Efficient concerns how resources are used; a method can work while using a great deal of time or energy.

originalSense.definition: Having the power to produce a required effect or effects.
originalSense.example: The pill is an effective method of birth control.

distinctionTask.prompt: A filter removes the dust it is intended to remove, but uses a lot of power. Calling it effective says it _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Effectiveness concerns the result. Resource use requires a separate judgement of efficiency.

restoreCorrections.definition: Producing a strong or decisive impression or effect.
restoreCorrections.example: The speaker used an effective pause before the final sentence.
distinctions: Here effective describes the impact of a speech or presentation. It does not describe the date on which a rule starts to apply.

originalSense.definition: Producing a decided or decisive effect.
originalSense.example: The president delivered an effective speech!

distinctionTask.prompt: A well-timed pause made the final sentence more memorable. The pause was effective because of its _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: In a presentation, an effective pause has the desired impact.

restoreCorrections.definition: Actually usable, operative or available for a stated purpose, rather than merely nominal.
restoreCorrections.example: The unit has an effective strength of fifty soldiers.
distinctions: Effective strength counts personnel actually available for duty, not merely a nominal total. Other uses include income actually available after stated deductions. The adjective does not by itself quantify energy efficiency.

originalSense.definition: Efficient, serviceable, or operative, available for useful work.
originalSense.example: How long does it take to make a bunch of civilians an effective military force?

distinctionTask.prompt: The unit lists eighty names, but only fifty soldiers are available for duty. Its effective strength is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Effective strength concerns the personnel actually available, rather than the nominal roster. The numbers are illustrative.

restoreCorrections.definition: In force or applying from a stated time.
restoreCorrections.example: The new timetable is effective from Monday.
distinctions: Effective from gives the starting time at which a rule or arrangement applies. It does not claim that the arrangement has already achieved its intended results.

originalSense.definition: Actually in effect.
originalSense.example: effective immediately

distinctionTask.prompt: The policy is effective from Monday. Monday is when it _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The phrase states when the policy comes into force, not whether it succeeds.

restoreCorrections.definition: In geometry, of a divisor or cycle, having only nonnegative coefficients.
restoreCorrections.example: An effective divisor can have positive or zero coefficients; a negative coefficient would violate this condition.
distinctions: Nonnegative includes zero. This specialised mathematical meaning does not mean a divisor that uses little energy.

originalSense.definition: Having no negative coefficients.

restoreCorrections.definition: Of a group action, having only the identity element act trivially on every point.
restoreCorrections.example: In an effective group action, every nonidentity element moves at least one point; the identity still fixes every point.
distinctions: The preserved gloss omits the identity exception. The identity always fixes every point. An effective action may allow a nonidentity element to fix some points, provided it does not fix all of them; a free action is a stronger condition.

originalSense.definition: Such that no group element acts trivially.

restoreCorrections.definition: In physics, describing a system approximately within a specified regime without representing every underlying process explicitly.
restoreCorrections.example: An effective theory describes the behaviour relevant to its intended regime while leaving some underlying details implicit.
distinctions: Approximate does not mean necessarily useless or inaccurate for the stated purpose. The theory has a limited regime of validity; this sense does not simply mean a law that has taken effect.

originalSense.definition: approximate; Not describing the fundamental dynamic changes in some system as they happen.

restoreCorrections.definition: In military use, a soldier fit and available for duty.
restoreCorrections.example: The preserved military quotation counts effectives: soldiers available for duty, rather than successful effects.
distinctions: This countable military noun names personnel. It is distinct from the adjective effective and from the plural noun effects.

originalSense.definition: a soldier fit for duty
originalSense.example: The Army of the West reached Corinth sometime after the battle of Shiloh. We were 15,000 effectives, and brought Beauregard's effective force up to 45,000 men.

restoreCorrections.definition: Using time, energy, money or other resources with little waste.
restoreCorrections.example: An efficient process uses less time for the same task.
distinctions: Efficient concerns resource use relative to the work done. Effective concerns achieving the intended result; the two judgements need not coincide.

originalSense.definition: Making good, thorough, or careful use of resources; not consuming extra. Especially, making good use of time or energy.
originalSense.example: An efficient process would automate all the routine work.

distinctionTask.prompt: Two processes complete the same task equally well; one takes half the time. Calling it more efficient compares _____.
options: resource use for the work done
the date on which a rule applies
distinctionTask.answer: resource use for the work done
distinctionTask.explanation: With the result held equal, lower time use supports the efficiency comparison.

restoreCorrections.definition: Converting a stated proportion of energy input into useful output.
restoreCorrections.example: The motor is 20 percent efficient under these test conditions.
collocations: the ratio of useful output to input
distinctions: If 100 joules enter and 20 joules become useful output, the efficiency is 20 percent. The remaining energy is transferred in other forms; it does not disappear. Conditions and the definition of useful output matter.

originalSense.definition: Expressing the proportion of consumed energy that was successfully used in a process; the ratio of useful output to total input.
originalSense.example: The motor is only 20% efficient at that temperature.

distinctionTask.prompt: A motor receives 100 joules and delivers 20 joules of useful output. Its efficiency is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Useful output divided by input is 20/100, or 20 percent. The other 80 joules are not useful output in this example.

restoreCorrections.definition: In the expression efficient cause, bringing about an effect or change.
restoreCorrections.example: An efficient cause is the cause or agent bringing an effect about; efficient here does not mean economical with resources.
distinctions: The philosophical and legal expression retains a causation sense. It is separate from the modern resource-use meaning; identifying a legal cause also requires the rules and facts of the case.
restoreCorrections.usage: Especially philosophy and specialised legal expression; contextual reading.

originalSense.definition: Causing effects, producing results; bringing into being; initiating change (rare except in philosophical and legal expression efficient cause = causative factor or agent).
originalSense.example: Ownership, maintenance, or use of the automobile need not be the direct and efficient cause of the injury sustained

restoreCorrections.definition: In older use, effective or capable of producing an effect.
restoreCorrections.example: The preserved poetic efficient blow means a blow that produces the intended effect.
distinctions: The source labels this an older, disputed use. For ordinary modern resource-use comparisons, distinguish efficient from effective rather than treating them as interchangeable.

originalSense.definition: effective, efficacious
originalSense.example:
Ye wake no more to anguish;‥ ye have borne
The Chosen, the Destroyer!‥ soon his hand
Shall strike the efficient blow;
Soon shaking off your penal forms, shall ye,
With songs of joy, amid the Eden groves,
Hymn the Deliverer’s praise!

restoreCorrections.definition: In obsolete use, a cause or something that produces an effect.
restoreCorrections.example: The preserved philosophical noun efficient names a cause, rather than a person who works quickly.
distinctions: This is an obsolete noun. The familiar modern adjective in an efficient worker is a different grammatical use.

originalSense.definition: A cause; something that causes an effect.
originalSense.example: Some are without efficient, as God; others without matter, as Angels […].

restoreCorrections.definition: Showing good judgement or making reasonable decisions.
restoreCorrections.example: Taking an umbrella was a sensible decision.
distinctions: Sensible concerns good judgement. Sensitive can describe being easily hurt, considerate or responsive; it is not a synonym for reasonable.

originalSense.definition: Acting with or showing good sense; able to make good judgements based on reason or wisdom, or reflecting such ability.
originalSense.example: They ask questions of someone who thinks he's got something sensible to say on some matter when actually he hasn't.

distinctionTask.prompt: Taking an umbrella because rain is forecast is a sensible decision: it shows _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The decision is reasonable in the circumstances. Sensible is distinct from sensitive.

restoreCorrections.definition: Practical or comfortable rather than chosen mainly for appearance or fashion.
restoreCorrections.example: She wore sensible shoes for the long walk.
distinctions: Sensible shoes suit the practical task and comfort needs. This does not require them to be unattractive, and it does not mean shoes that detect small changes.

originalSense.definition: Characterized more by usefulness, practicality, or comfort than by attractiveness, formality, or fashionableness, especially of clothing.
originalSense.example: I only wear high heels on formal occasions; otherwise, I prefer sensible shoes.

distinctionTask.prompt: Sensible shoes for a long walk are selected mainly for _____.
options: an ability to register small changes
distinctionTask.explanation: The clothing sense concerns suitability for the task and comfort, without requiring an unattractive appearance.

restoreCorrections.definition: Able to be perceived through the senses or mental experience.
restoreCorrections.example: Sensible objects can be perceived through the senses.
distinctions: This formal perceptibility sense differs from wise or practical. An object described as sensible in a discussion of perception is not being credited with good judgement.

originalSense.definition: Able to be sensed by the senses or the psyche; able to be perceived.
originalSense.example: For Plato the belief in sensible objects is fallible.

distinctionTask.prompt: In a philosophical discussion, sensible objects are objects that can be _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The formal sense concerns perceptibility, rather than good judgement.

restoreCorrections.definition: In archaic use, capable of feeling or perceiving.
restoreCorrections.example: The preserved Shakespeare passage wishes that cambric could be sensible as a finger is: able to feel.
distinctions: The older adjective describes capacity for sensation, rather than a reasonable decision or practical clothing.

originalSense.definition: Able to feel or perceive.
originalSense.example: Would your cambric were sensible as your finger.

restoreCorrections.definition: In archaic use, easily affected by external impressions; sensitive.
restoreCorrections.example: The source’s sensible thermometer means an instrument readily affected by changes.
distinctions: Modern technical English ordinarily uses sensitive for responsiveness. The older sensible use does not mean the instrument exercises good judgement.

originalSense.definition: Liable to external impression; easily affected; sensitive.
originalSense.example: a sensible thermometer

restoreCorrections.definition: In archaic use, relating to the senses; sensory.
restoreCorrections.example: The source’s older sensory sense of sensible concerns perception through the senses.
distinctions: Sensory concerns the senses; sensible in ordinary decision-making concerns good judgement. The historical overlap does not make the two modern uses freely interchangeable.

originalSense.definition: Of or pertaining to the senses; sensory.

restoreCorrections.definition: In older use, aware of or conscious of something.
restoreCorrections.example: In the preserved Locke passage, being sensible of thinking means being aware of it.
distinctions: The construction sensible of retains an awareness sense in older and formal writing. It does not mean that the thing perceived is a wise decision.
restoreCorrections.usage: Source labels this archaic; contextual reading.

originalSense.definition: Cognizant; having the perception of something; aware of something.
originalSense.example: He cannot think at any time, waking or sleeping, without being sensible of it.

restoreCorrections.definition: In obsolete use, sensation or the capacity for feeling.
restoreCorrections.example: The source’s sensible of pain names a sensation or feeling of pain.
distinctions: This obsolete noun concerns feeling. It is not the modern adjective in a sensible response.

originalSense.definition: Sensation; sensibility.
originalSense.example: Our temper changed […] which must needs remove the sensible of pain.

restoreCorrections.definition: In obsolete use, something perceptible or capable of impressing itself on the senses.
restoreCorrections.example: The preserved Aristotle-related example uses sensibles for things perceived through the senses.
distinctions: The plural sensibles here names objects or qualities of perception. It does not mean a group of people with good judgement.

originalSense.definition: That which impresses itself on the senses; anything perceptible.
originalSense.example: Aristotle distinguished sensibles into common and proper.

restoreCorrections.definition: In obsolete use, a being capable of sensation or feeling.
restoreCorrections.example: The preserved passage groups sensibles as beings capable of feeling or perception.
distinctions: The old noun classifies beings by capacity for sensation, rather than judging their decisions or claiming paranormal powers.

originalSense.definition: That which has sensibility; a sensitive being.
originalSense.example: This melancholy extends itself not to men only, but even to vegetals and sensibles.

restoreCorrections.definition: Having the capacity for sensation or relating to the senses.
restoreCorrections.example: The preserved sensitive faculty refers to the capacity for sensation, rather than to hurt feelings.
distinctions: This general sensory sense underlies some older and philosophical uses. Do not replace every occurrence with easily upset.
restoreCorrections.usage: Sensory or philosophical context; reading note.

originalSense.definition: Having the faculty of sensation; pertaining to the senses.
originalSense.example: The sensitive faculty most part overrules reason, the soul is carried hoodwinked, and the understanding captive like a beast.

restoreCorrections.definition: Responding readily to particular stimuli or influences.
restoreCorrections.example: Some plants are sensitive to changes in temperature.
distinctions: Sensitive to identifies what produces a response. A responsive plant or material need not have hurt feelings or make a sensible decision.

originalSense.definition: Responsive to stimuli.
originalSense.example: The engine seemed a little sensitive to wet rails, and in consequence the uphill work was not so good north of Dundee as it had been earlier. But I have noted this same "touchiness" on the part of the "A4s", and other modern British 4-6-2s, so that in this respect No. 2006 proved no exception.

distinctionTask.prompt: A plant changes its response when the temperature changes. Sensitive here means _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Temperature is the influence to which the plant responds.

restoreCorrections.definition: Easily affected emotionally by criticism or other people’s words and actions.
restoreCorrections.example: He is sensitive to criticism.
distinctions: The person is readily hurt or upset. Being sensitive can also mean considerate of others, but that is a separate sense and is not established by this sentence.

originalSense.definition: Easily offended, upset, or hurt.
originalSense.example: Max is very sensitive; he cried today because of the bad news.

distinctionTask.prompt: He is sensitive to criticism. This says he is _____.
options: necessarily careful not to hurt anyone else
distinctionTask.explanation: The phrase describes his own emotional response. Consideration for others is another sense.

restoreCorrections.definition: Of a topic or issue, capable of causing offence, distress or hurt.
restoreCorrections.example: Pay can be a sensitive topic at work.
distinctions: The topic may upset people or need tact. This does not mean that every discussion is forbidden, or that the topic itself has feelings.

originalSense.definition: Capable of offending, upsetting, or hurting.
originalSense.example: Religion is often a sensitive topic of discussion and should be avoided when dealing with foreign business associates.

distinctionTask.prompt: Pay is a sensitive topic at work because discussion may _____.
options: mean that the topic has emotions
distinctionTask.explanation: A sensitive issue may affect people emotionally; the issue itself does not feel.

restoreCorrections.definition: Intended to be kept private or disclosed only to appropriate people.
restoreCorrections.example: The file contains sensitive personal information.
distinctions: Here sensitive concerns confidentiality. It does not mean that the documents feel offended, and the adjective alone does not establish a particular legal classification.

originalSense.definition: Meant to be concealed or kept secret.
originalSense.example: These are highly sensitive documents.

distinctionTask.prompt: Only authorised staff may read the sensitive file. Sensitive refers to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Access restrictions identify the confidential-information sense.

restoreCorrections.definition: Aware of other people’s feelings and careful to avoid unnecessary hurt.
restoreCorrections.example: Please be sensitive to other people’s feelings.
distinctions: This considerate sense concerns how someone treats others. It differs from being easily hurt oneself, though a person can have both qualities.

originalSense.definition: Being aware of the feelings of others and taking care not to offend them.
originalSense.example: Thank you for being sensitive.

distinctionTask.prompt: She chose her words carefully to be sensitive to his feelings. She was being _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The action shows care for another person, rather than stating her own vulnerability.

restoreCorrections.definition: Requiring especially careful or tactful handling because it is delicate or consequential.
restoreCorrections.example: These sensitive negotiations require careful wording.
distinctions: The work or situation needs care. It need not involve secret documents or a highly responsive measuring device.

originalSense.definition: Important, intricate, and requiring great delicacy.
originalSense.example: The president's untimely statement disrupted some very sensitive negotiations.

distinctionTask.prompt: Sensitive negotiations require carefully chosen wording. Sensitive means _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Negotiations are a delicate situation. The instrument sense requires a different context.

restoreCorrections.definition: Of a measuring instrument, able to detect or respond to small changes in what it measures.
restoreCorrections.example: The sensitive instrument can register a small change in pressure.
distinctions: The preserved gloss also says accurate, but sensitivity does not by itself guarantee accuracy. In metrology, sensitivity relates a change in indication to a change in the measured quantity; accuracy concerns agreement with a true value.

originalSense.definition: Accurate; able to register small changes in some property.

distinctionTask.prompt: A detector responds to a very small input change, but has a calibration bias. Its sensitivity proves _____.
options: responsiveness, without by itself proving accuracy
that its readings must equal the true value
distinctionTask.answer: responsiveness, without by itself proving accuracy
distinctionTask.explanation: Sensitivity and accuracy answer different questions. A biased instrument can still respond strongly to small changes.

restoreCorrections.definition: In an archaic paranormal context, said to have abilities that could be controlled through mesmerism.
restoreCorrections.example: The source’s older sensitive adjective belongs to accounts of alleged paranormal abilities and mesmerism.
distinctions: This records a historical belief and word use. The dictionary description does not establish that the claimed paranormal ability exists.

originalSense.definition: Having paranormal abilities that can be controlled through mesmerism.

restoreCorrections.definition: A person said to have a paranormal sensitivity that most people do not have.
restoreCorrections.example: The preserved quotation calls some people sensitives in a paranormal or mediumistic context.
distinctions: This noun records how a person is described in such accounts. It does not verify paranormal abilities, and it is separate from the ordinary adjective for a considerate or easily hurt person.

originalSense.definition: A person with a paranormal sensitivity to something that most cannot perceive.
originalSense.example: [I]t is quite certain that many of their fears were unfounded, and centred upon perfectly innocent people - especially those who were what we now call "mediumistic" or "sensitives".
